content: 1. Why JWT? The problem with sessions: every time you log in, the server creates a session and gives you back a session ID (e.g. 102 -> session id ). As long as you hold that ID, you don’t need to log in again and again – but constantly re-authenticating everywhere isn’t always good , especially across different services. Coffee shop analogy: - Yash pays $50 for a subscription at a coffee shop (Bob). - In return, he gets an id/token for that subscription – containing things like id , name , issue date , expiry date . - Next time (say, Mahesh), he just shows this token/id to get coffee – no need to pay or re-verify from scratch each time. - Risk: if someone fakes/copies this token , they could also get coffee with it – so the token itself needs to be trustworthy and verifiable. Representing this token as data: - We could use XML , but XML is bulky, and encrypting it produces an even bulkier output. - Alternative: JSON – lightweight, and compresses better after encryption. - So: data (as JSON) + encryption -> Token -> JWT . Real-world use – Single Sign-On (SSO): using a token from one login (e.g. Gmail), you can log in to other apps of the same provider (e.g. other Google apps) without logging in again – this is Single Sign-On (SSO) . 2.
